full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed J: The mainstay of the prayer for a Rule Nisi has been the ratio decidendi of the Appellate Division Judgment in Khaledur Reza Chowdhury vs Saleha Begum, reported in 48 DLR (AD) 268 as authored by Mustafa Kama J as he was then. The moot issue arising in this case therefore is of the substantive status and effect of an order of conviction and sentence during the pendency of an appeal. The petitioner's learned Advocate, Mr AJ Mohammad All has argued on the 48 DLR case as authority for the view that an electoral disqualification stemming from a conviction and sentence would only mature become final either on a final disposal of an appeal or an expiration of the limitation period of filing of appeal. Mr Mahbubey Alam appearing for the Election Commission has gone on to contradict that position. Mr Alam's assertion on the contrary has been that the 48 DLR Case remains authority instead for a limited exercise of authority in judicial review by a constitutional court in matters of election disputes. He has also cited the judgment in Zahedul Islam Khan vs HM Ershad, reported in 6 BLC 301 as upheld in Hussain Mohammad Ershad vs Zahidul Islam Khan, reported in 21 BLD (AD) 142 = 54 DLR (AD) 1 as indicative of a dis-qualification attaching immediately upon conviction in the context of Article 66(2) (d) of the Constitution.

2. The debate above demonstrates to this Court and in the undersigned's considered opinion a lack or absence of a definitive and entrenched judicial view expressed in particular by the Appellate Division on the nature of disqualification attaching upon a conviction in the context of Article 66(2)(d) of the Constitution and the substantive effects following therefrom. That in itself in the undersigned's view merits a Rule Nisi to be issued for fundamental for constitutional issues to be thrashed out in judicial review. Furthermore, it has not escaped this judge's attention that the impugned order of rejection by the Respondent No. 3 Deputy Commissioner and Returning Officer, Feni is substantively flawed in its citation of a disqualifying provision of the RPO evidently inapplicable in the facts and that the other impugned order of 8-12-2018 issued by the Respondent No. 1, Election Commission Bangladesh affirming such rejection and cancellation order of 2-12-2018 is not a unanimous one. Indeed a dissenting order of one Election Commissioner is on record questioning the sufficiency of the rejection order of 2-12-2018 passed by the Respondent No. 3. These facts also further attest to the need for further review of all relevant issues by this Court.

3. There is additionally an element of the petitioner potentially being treated in a manner that is in contravention of fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 27 in particular of the Constitution given her contention that certain individuals otherwise similarly placed as her have been allowed to contest the forthcoming election.

4. Predicated on the above an entire gamut of issues convinces the undersigned that the issue of disqualification that is focal to this case arising from a conviction and sentence is far from being a settled matter authoritatively and definitively decided upon by the superior court at any level.

5. With jurisprudence so unevolved and a dearth of judicial precedents so pronounced concerning the issue of disqualification as arises here the merit in this application under Article 102 lies at the end of the day in offering an opportunity to establish a definitive judicial stance on such issue. Until then the under-signed sees no ground that can reasonably be taken to satisfactorily apply any ostensible objective standard with any level of certainty in the facts and circumstances. To argue and insist otherwise would be to take an overly formalistic view of the application of the relevant law and constitutional provision.

<u>6. Furthermore, to summarily reject this application in the absence of any definitive judicial endorsement of a standard test applicable across a broad spectrum of cases would result in offending the entrenched constitutional equality and anti-discrimination standards preventing jurisprudential development and authoritative interpretation of Article 66(2)(d) and stunting, resultantly, the growth of a substantive democratic order beyond a mere formal one. A final and authoritative ruling on the interpretation of application of Article 66(2)(d) therefore warrants a full scale hearing of the matter which in turn necessitates the issuance of Rule Nisi.</u>

7. That being the case and upon prima facie satisfaction of the merit of this Application let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why (i) the petitioner should not allowed to participate in the ensuing national parliamentary elections on 30 December 2018 pursuant to a decision of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh reported in 48 DLR (AD) 208 (Annexure2D) and (ii) why decisions passed by the Respondent No. 3 rejecting and cancelling the nomination paper of the Petitioner on 2-12-18 and affirmed by the Respondent No. 1 on 8-12-18 for participating in the ensuing 11th national parliamentary elections on 30th December 2018 from the electoral constituency 265 Feni-1 should not be declared to have been passed illegally, without lawful authority and is of no legal effect in view of the decision of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh reported in 48 DLR (AD) 208 (Annexure-'C') and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

8. Let the operation of the impugned decisions passed by the Respondent No. 3 cancelling the nomination paper of the Petitioner on 2-12-2018 and affirmed by the Respondent No. 1 on 8-12-2018 in Election Appeal No. 440/2018 for participating in the ensuing 11th national parliamentary elections on 30th December 2018 from the electoral constituency 265 Feni-1 be stayed for a period of 3 (three) months from date.

9. Furthermore, the Respondents are directed to allow the Petitioner to complete all necessary formalities to contest in the upcoming 11th parliamentary elections from 265 Feni-1 electoral Constituency beyond the timeline otherwise fixed by the Respondents.

10. The Rule is made returnable within 2 (two) weeks from date.

11. The Petitioner shall put in necessary requisites for service of notices upon all the Respondents by special messenger.

Iqbal Kabir j: I have privilege of hearing of the order just passed by his Lordship Mr Justice Syed Refaat Ahmed with great respect to his deliberation. But I regret, I could not pursued myself to agree with the view taken by his Lordship in deciding above noted writ petition. I have different view and disinclined to do so for the following reasons:

13. In the present writ petition the petitioner upon relying a decision passed in the case of AKM Mayeedul Islam vs Bangladesh Election Commission, reported in 48 DLR (AD) 208, filed this writ petition claiming that the issue of conviction as of Article 66(2)(d) has been settled by that decision. But my considered view is that the said issue about the conviction has not been settled by the said judgment. Because of that in this regard the legend lawyer of this arena Mr. Mahmudul Islam in his book titled as the Constitutional Law of Bangladesh, in chapter four of 4.6A clearly states—

"A question arises as to the interpretation of the expression 'conviction' in Article 66(2)(d)—whether it means conviction by the trial court or it means conviction which has become final and conclusive on appeal to the highest court. When HM Ershad became a candidate for the parliamentary election in 1996 while he was serving his sentence during the pendency of the appeal before the High Court Division the question arose as to whether he was disqualified because of his conviction. The Returning Officer found his nomination paper invalid and the matter came up before the Appellate Division in Mayeedul Islam vs Bangladesh Election Commission, but the court did not answer the question and merely observed that it was for the Election Commission to decide an election Dispute".

14. At the same time in a decision passed in the case of Hussain Mohammad Ershad vs Zahedul Islam, reported in 21 BLD (AD) 142 = 54 DLR (AD) 1 our apex Court quoting the above Article 66(2)(d) of the Constitution clearly held that from this Article it appears that a person shall be disqualified for election who has been convicted for a criminal offence involving moral turpitude and sentenced to imprisonment for a term of not less than two years unless a period of five years has elapsed since his release.

<u>15. In this writ petition petitioner has challenged the order passed by the concerned Returning Officer cancelling her nomination on the ground that the petitioner was convicted in Special Case No. 3 of 2010 arising out of Ramna Police Station Case No. 8(7) 2008 and accordingly sentenced to imprisonment for 5 (five) years under section 409/109 of the Penal Code and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 though the said sentence was ultimately enhanced to 10 years by the High Court Division and in Special Case No. 18 of 2017 arising out of Tejgaon Police Station Case No. 15(08)2011 the petitioner was sentenced to imprisonment for 7 (seven) years. It was held that she was debarred from contesting parliamentary election in view of the provision under Article 66(2)(d) of the Constitution. In the appeal before the Election Commission the petitioner tried to convince the commission by referring to a decision reported in 48 DLR (AD) 208. However, Election Commission dismissed the appeal and thereby affirmed the order of the Returning Officer by which Returning Officer cancelled her nomination paper. It is the admitted position that the present petitioner is a convicted person and the conviction against the petitioner has not been interfered with either by suspension or setting aside by any competent Court of this Country. More particularly the petitioner did not have taken any proper steps in this regard to stay the said convictions. Therefore, the said convictions are still operative. It is to be noted here that according to the prevailing law there is no provision to suspend the order of conviction passed by the trial Court. Moreover, as per Article 66(2)(d) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh a person who is convicted for criminal offence involving moral turpitude and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for a term of not less than two years will be disqualified for election as a Member of Parliament unless a period of five years has elapsed since his/her release. And thus, the constitutional provision cannot override.</u>

16. Moreover, while a convicted person by filling Writ Petition No. 15639 of 2018 sought to participate in the upcoming national parliament election as she was debarred in view of the provision under Article 66(2)(d) of the Constitution. A Division Bench of this Court summarily rejected the said writ petition upholding the decision of the election commission.

17. In the cited decision reported in 48 DLR (AD) 208 our Apex Court clearly states that writ Court can only interfere when the impugned order passed by the authority concerned is coram non judice or is afflicted with malice in law. Thus, I do not find any scope to interfere with the order as passed by the Election Commission in this particular case. Hence I find it is a misconceived application.

18. In premises, I do not find any merit in this application. Accordingly, the petition is rejected, summarily.

Editor's Note: The Hon'ble Judges of the Division Bench having delivered dissenting order, the matter was referred, as per rule of practice, to a third Judge Mr JBM Hassan J for disposal. Hassan, J delivered the following order.

High Court Division

(Special Original Jurisdiction)

JBM Hassan J

Writ Petition No.15741 of 2018

Begum Khaleda Zia-------Petitioner

Vs

Bangladesh Election Commission represented by the Chief Election Commissioner, Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka-------Respondents

Order December 18th, 2018

Order

JBM Hassan J: This is an application filed by the petitioner for sending back the writ petition No. 15741 of 2018 to the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh.

21. Referring to the statements as made in paragraphs No. 4, 5 and 12 of the application, the learned advocate for the petitioner submits that the writ petition was heard by Mr Justice Syed Refaat Ahmed as presiding judge of a Division Bench and so after dissenting order, it should be heard by a judge senior to Mr Justice Syed Refaat Ahmed. In the circumstances, Mr Ali makes prayer to send back the writ petition to the Hon'ble Chief Justice.

22. On the other hand Mr Mahabubey Alam, the learned Senior Advocate for the Election Commission contends that under the Constitution all the judges of the High Court Division are equal and that there is no such rules as claimed by the learned advocate for the petitioner. He refers to a series of examples, among others writ petition No. 5556 of 2014 (Shawkat Hossain vs Government of Bangladesh and others) popularly known as Nizam Uddin Hazari's (a former member of parliament) case a dissenting judgment was passed by a Division Bench presided over by Mr Justice Md Abu Zafor Siddique who was elevated to the bench long after elevation of Mr Justice Md Emdadul Haq.

23. This Court has gone through the application and considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for the contending parties.

24. In view of a dissenting order, the Hon'ble Chief Justice has sent this writ petition before this Bench by an order dated 12-12-2018 for hearing and disposal of the matter. Therefore, this Court cannot send it back to the Hon'ble Chief Justice. The petitioner could make such prayer before the Hon'ble Chief Justice but she did not do so. Hence, this Court does not entertain the misconceived application for sending back the writ petition to the Hon'ble Chief Justice. Accordingly the application is rejected as being not maintainable.

25. The learned advocates for the petitioner are directed to make submissions on merit of the writ petition.

26. This is an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

27. The petitioner, Begum Khaleda Zia has filed this writ petition challenging the order dated 8-12-2018 passed by the Bangladesh Election Commission (respondent No. 1) in Appeal No. 385 of 2018 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the order dated 2-12-2018 of the retuning officer, Feni cancelling nomination paper of the petitioner offering her candidature from the Electoral Constituency No. 265, Feni-1 in the ensuing 11th Parliamentary Election scheduled to be held on 30-12-2018 on the ground of conviction relating to criminal offences involving moral turpitude and sentences thereunder of more than two years.

28. The writ petition was heard by a Division Bench comprised of Mr Justice Syed Refaat Ahmed and Mr Justice Md Iqbal Kabir. Upon hearing, by order dated 11-12-2018 Mr Justice Syed Refaat Ahmed issued a Rule Nisi with an interim order staying operation of the impugned order of the Election Commission dated 8-12-2018 affirming the order dated 2-12-2018 of the Returning Office cancelling nomination paper of the petitioner. His Lordship also directed the respondents to allow the petitioner to complete all necessary formalities to contest upcoming 11th parliamentary election from Electoral Constituency No. 265, Feni-1. On the other hand, Mr Justice Md Iqbal Kabir by his dissenting order rejected the writ petition summarily.

29. At this juncture, the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh by order dated 12-12-2018 sent this matter to this Bench for hearing and disposal.

30. Accordingly, the matter was posted for hearing in the daily cause list on the very next day i.e. on 13-12-2018 at 2-00 pm but hearing was adjourned for the day on the prayer of Mr AJ Mohammad Ali the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner. Mr Ali also submitted that he would make prayer before the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh for taking the matter for hearing before a learned Judge who is senior to Mr Justice Syed Refaat Ahmed, a party to the dissenting order. On the next opening day i.e. on 17-12-2018 at 10-30 am when the matter was taken up for hearing at the very outset, the leaned Advocate for the petitioner made prayer for adjournment of hearing until 2-00 pm in order to make an appropriate prayer before the Hon'ble Chief Justice for constituting a new Bench. Accordingly as per prayer of the learned Advocate the matter was adjourned until 2-00 pm. But at 2-00 pm the learned Advocate for the Petitioner again submitted that they could not make prayer before the Hon'ble Chief Justice and hence again sought adjournment of hearing of the matter. On the prayer of the learned Advocate for the petitioner again the matter was adjourned for the day and accordingly, today the last working day before winter vacation, this matter has appeared in the daily cause list for hearing.

31. At the very outset, Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner has placed an application for sending back the writ petition to the Hon'ble Chief Justice. Since this matter has been sent to this Bench by the Hon'ble Justice for hearing and disposal of the writ petition this Court cannot send it to him back. But the learned Advocate for the petitioner instead of making such prayer before the Hon'ble Chief Justice was taking adjournments one after another and lastly the misconceived application for sending back the writ petition being filed before this Bench it was rejected as being not maintainable by a separate order and at the same time this Court directed the petitioner's learned Advocates to make submissions on merit of the writ petition.

32. At this stage, the learned Advocate for the petitioner in particular Mr AJ Mohammad All the learned Senior Advocate with Mr Md Bodrudduza and Mr AHM Kamruzzaman, the learned Advocates again made prayer for adjournment of hearing of the writ petition without mentioning any new reason for adjournment except for the reason stated in the application which was rejected earlier by this Court.

33. This writ petition relates to determination of candidature of the petitioner in the ensuing election scheduled to be held on 3-12-2018. Although the writ petition has already been placed by the petitioner's learned Advocate before a Division Bench and upon hearing a dissenting order was passed in order to make it final the matter has been sent to this Bench by the Hon'ble Chief Justice. In this situation while the petitioner's learned Advocate was taking adjournments one after another, Mr Mahbubey Alam the learned Senior Advocate for the Election Commission vehemently opposes the prayer for adjournment contending that the issue as to candidature of petitioner has to be settled without delay inasmuch as the Election Commission has to take all sorts of preparation including printing of ballot papers relating to three electoral constituencies concerning petitioner's candidature for the ensuing election scheduled to be held on 30-12-2018 and on the other hand the Court is going on winter vacation today. In the circumstances, considering all aspects this Court rejected the prayer made by the petitioner's learned Advocate without mentioning any cogent reason for adjournment and directed the learned Advocates for the petitioner to make submissions on merit of the writ petition but the learned Advocates did not come forward to make their submissions.

34. However, Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the Election Commission has placed the writ petition and other materials on record. Mr. Mahabubey Alam submits that admittedly the petitioner is a convicted person in two criminal cases being Special Cases No. 17 of 2017 and 18 of 2017 relating to offences involving moral turpitude and she was awarded sentences thereunder of more than two years in each case. Therefore, she is disqualified to participate in the ensuing parliamentary election in accordance with Article 66(2)(d) of the Constitution. He further submits that although the petitioner preferred Criminal Appeal No. 12374 of 2018 against the conviction and sentence passed in Special Cases No. 18 of 2017 but pendency of such appeal shall not ipso facto make the conviction non-operative and so the Election Commission rightly cancelled her nomination paper which does not call for any interference. Mr Alam next submits that the conviction and sentence awarded in Special Case No. 17 of 2017 (previous number 03 of 2010) have been affirmed by the High Court Division and that Criminal Miscellaneous Petition for Leave to Appeal is not an appeal. He also submits that the ratio laid down in 48 DLR (AD) 208 is not applicable in the present case and that the consistent view of the Appellate Division in the recent cases relating to ensuing parliamentary election is that pendency of criminal appeal cannot be considered for qualifying a convict to participate in the election in view of Article 66(2)(d) of the Constitution.

35. This Court has gone through the writ petition along with its annexure including the orders in question i.e. cancellation order of nomination paper passed by the Returning Officer as well as the order of the Election Commission passed in the appeal, the dissenting order dated 11-12-2018 as well as the cases reported in 48 DLR (AD) 208 and 21 BLD (AD) 142 = 54 DLR (AD) 1.

36. It appears from the writ petition that the petitioner was entangled in Special Case No. 17 of 2017 (previous number 03 of 2010) arising out of Ramna Police Station Case No. 08 dated 3-7-2018, After conclusion of trial by the judgment and order dated 8-2-2018 she was convicted under sections 409/109 of the Penal Code as well as under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 (II of 1947). However, sentence was passed only under sections 409/109 of the Penal Code to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 5 (five) years. Challenging the said conviction and sentence the petitioner preferred Criminal Appeal No. 1679 of 2018 and eventually it was dismissed by the judgment and order dated 30-10-2018 of the High Court Division affirming the conviction and enhancing the sentence to 10 (ten) years. Against the said judgment and order of conviction and sentence the petitioner filed Criminal Miscellaneous Petitions for Leave to Appeal No. 1524 of 2018 and 1525 of 2018 which are now pending before the Appellate Division.

37. It further appears that another case being Special Case No. 18 of 2017 arose out of Tejgaon Police Station Case No. 15 dated 8-8-2011 was initiated against the petitioner and others and that ultimately by the judgment and order dated 29-10-2018 the petitioner was convicted under section 5(2) of the Act 1947 and sentenced thereunder to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 7 (seven) years and to pay a fine of Taka 10 (ten) lac in default to suffer simple imprisonment for six months. Against the said judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 29-10-2018 the petitioner preferred Criminal Appeal No. 12374 of 2018 which is now pending before the High Court Division.

38. Referring to the aforesaid convictions and sentence under two criminal case relating to offences involving moral turpitude, the Returning Officer cancelled the nomination paper of the petitioner offering her candidature in the ensuing 11th Parliamentary Election from the Constituency No. 265 Feni-01. Against the said cancellation order the petitioner preferred Appeal No. 385 of 2018 before the Election Commission and by the impugned order dated 8-12-2018 the Appeal was dismissed affirming the cancellation order passed by the Returning Officer.

39. Therefore, question arise as to whether the petitioner will be allowed to participate in the ensuing parliamentary election which is scheduled to be held on 30-12-2018 for the mentioned constituency. In this regard the legal obstruction being the Article 66(2)(d) of the Constitution of the People's Republic Bangladesh this Court has taken a look at the said Article 66(2)(d) which runs as follows:

“সংসদে নির্বাচিত হইবার যোগ্যতা ও অযোগ্যতাঃ

৬৬।(১)…………..

(২) কোন ব্যক্তি সংসদের সদস্য নির্বাচিত হইবার এবং সংসদ-সদস্য থাকিবার যোগ্য হইবেন না, যদি

(ক)-(গ)………………..

(ঘ) তিনি নৈতিক স্থলনজনিত কোন ফৌজদারী অপরাধে দোষী সাব্যস্ত হইয়া অন্যূন বৎসরের কারাদন্ডে দন্ডিত হন এবং তাঁহার মুক্তিলাভের পর পাঁচ বৎসরের কারাদন্ডে দন্ডিত হন এবং তাঁহার মুক্তিলাভের পর পাঁচ বৎসরকাল অতিবাহিত না হইয়া থাকে;

(ঙ)-(ছ)……………

<u>40. Article 66(2)(d) of the Constitution makes it clear that a person shall be disqualified for election as a member of Parliament on conviction for a criminal offence involving moral turpitude and sentenced to imprisonment for a term of not less than two years. This legal proposition has been settled in the case of Hussain Mohammad Ershad vs Zahedul Islam Khan, reported in 21 BLD (AD) 142 = 54 DLR (AD) 1.</u>

41. Indisputably the petitioner was convicted in two criminal cases relating to offences involving moral turpitude and she was sentenced thereunder for more than two years in each case. But petitioner's contention is that since she preferred appeals against the said convictions and sentences, before coming to finality thereof in the appeals Article 66(2) of the Constitution shall not disqualify her candidature.

42. Since relying upon the case of AKM Mayeedul Islam vs Bangladesh Election Commission, reported in 48 DLR (AD) 208, the petitioner seeks Rule Nisi this Court has gone through the same. In this case the candidature of Hussain Mohammad Ershad was challenged on the ground of his conviction and sentence invoking Article 66(2)(d) of the Constitution. Although here the issue was raised as to the effect of pendency of appeals against the orders of conviction and sentence but the apex Court did not answer on this point leaving the same to the Election Tribunal in disposing of Election petition, if any, filed by the affected candidate. Therefore there being no ratio in the case reported in 48 DLR (AD) 208 relating to the issue in question, it does not help the petitioner in any manner albeit the petitioner seeks remedy relying on this case.

<u>43. It is the consistent view of our apex. Court is that although the execution of sentence can be suspended under section 426 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but conviction cannot be suspended in appeal for want of any legal prevision in the said Code. However, the conviction and sentence passed in Special Case No. 18 of 2017 has been challenged in Criminal Appeal No. 12374 of 2018 but there is no order of stay or suspension upon the impugned conviction and sentence. Therefore, the conviction awarded to the petitioner under section-5(2) of the Act, 1947 and sentence to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 7 (seven) years by the trial court in Special Case No. 18 of 2017 remains operative in spite of pendency of Criminal Appeal before the High Court Division and so this conviction and sentence disqualify the petitioner in participating the ensuing parliamentary election scheduled to be held on 30-12-2018.</u>

44. What is more in special Case No. 17 of 2017 (previous number 03 of 2010) the petitioner has been convicted relating to offence involving moral turpitude and she was sentenced thereunder to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 05 years by judgment and order dated 8-2-2018. Against the same the petitioner preferred Criminal Appeal No. 1667 of 2018 and ultimately by the judgment and order dated 30-10-2018 the appeal was dismissed with modification of sentence and thereby the conviction awarded by the trial Court has been confirmed and at the same time the sentence was enhanced to 10 years. Although against the said judgment and order the petitioner filed Criminal Miscellaneous Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1524 of 2018 under Article 103(3) of the Constitution but these petitions have not yet been heard At this juncture, question arises as to whether these Criminal Miscellaneous Petitions for Leave to Appeal can be treated as appeals of the petitioner. In this regard this Court finds the Article 103(3) of the Constitution which runs as follows:

“আপীল বিভাগের এখতিয়ারঃ

১০৩ । (১)………………

(২) হাইকোর্ট বিভাগের রায়, ডিক্রি, আদেশ বা দন্ডাদেশের বিরুদ্ধে আপীল বিভাগের নিকট সেই ক্ষেত্রে অধিকারবলে আপীল করা যাইবে, যে ক্ষেত্রে হাইকোর্ট বিভাগ

(ক) এই মর্মে সার্টিফিকেট দান করিবেন যে, মামলাটির সহিত এই সংবিধান-ব্যাখ্যার বিষয়ে আইনের

গুরুত্বপূর্ণ প্রশ্ন জড়িত রহিয়াছে; অথবা

(খ) কোন মৃত্যুদন্ড বহাল করিয়াছেন কিংবা কোন ব্যক্তিকে মৃত্যুদন্ডে বা যাবজ্জীবন কারাদন্ডে দন্ডিত করিয়াছেন

(গ) উক্ত বিভাগের অবমাননার জন্য কোন ব্যক্তিকে দন্ড দান করিয়াছেন ।

এবং সংসদে আইন দ্বারা যেরূপ বিধান করা হইবে, সেইরূপ অন্যান্য ক্ষেত্রে ।

(৩) হাইকোর্ট বিভাগের রায়, ডিক্রি, আদেশ বা দন্ডাদেশের বিরুদ্ধে যে মামলায় এই অনুচ্ছেদের (২) দফা প্রযোজ্য নহে, কেবল আপীল বিভাগ আপীলের অনুমতি দান করিলে সেই মামলায় আপীল চলিবে ।

<u>45. On a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions it is clear that am appeal shall only lie as of right under the circumstances as mentioned in sub-clauses (Ka), (Kha) and (Ga) of Article 103(2) of the Constitution and that except thereof in all other cases the aggrieved person has to file petition for leave to appeal under Article 103(3) of the Constitution and unless the Appellate Division grants leave in the appropriate petition for leave to appeal there cannot be any appeal.</u>

46. Here the petitioner has only filed Criminal Miscellaneous Petitions for Leave to Appeal being No. 1624 of 2018 and 1625 of 2018 and even she has not yet filed any regular Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal. After filing and hearing of the regular Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal if the Court grants leave, then appeal will be registered against the judgment of the High Court Division and it is yet to be done. Therefore, it is too far to consider petitioner's petition for leave to appeal as an appeal in accordance with the Article 103(3) of the Constitution.

<u>47. Regard being had to the above so far as the conviction and sentence awarded to the petitioner in Special Case No. 17 of 2017 (3 of 2010) and affirmed by the judgment and order of the High Court Division is concerned, the petitioner has no scope even to enter into any debate relating to the effect of pendency of appeal against the orders of conviction and sentence inasmuch as in the eye of law there is no appeal against the same as yet before the Appellate Division and so petitioner's conviction and sentence remains confirmed without any appeal and, as such, on this score as well as the petitioner is a disqualified person in the ensuing election in accordance with Article 66(2)(d) of the Constitution.</u>

48. Heaving regard to the above scenario this Court does not find any impropriety in the orders passed by both the Returning Officer as well as the Election Commission. Hence, there is no merit in this application.

Accordingly, the writ petition is rejected summarily.

End.

lawyer:
Mohammad Eunus, Advocate-------For the Petitioner.
Md Borhan Uddin, Advocate--------For the Opposite-Party.
parties:
Zabed Ali Howlader--------Petitioner
VS
Amzad Hossain--------Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This rule was issued at the instance of the plaintiff-respondent calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 8-11-2010 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Third Court, Patuakhali in Title Appeal No. 92 of 2009 reversing the judgment and decree dated 22-4-2009 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Mirzagonj in Title Suit No.30 of 2006.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 30 of 2006 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Mirzagonj, Patuakhali for redemption of the land more fully described in the schedule of the plaint.

3. Briefly stated the case of the plaintiff is that the land of Mouza Uttar Amragacia of SA Khatian No. 366 measuring an area of 0.20 decimals sold to defendant Amzad Hossain son of late Khadem Ali Hawlader by registered sale deed dated 27-3-1967 and on the same day an Ekrarnama was executed between the parties to reconvey the said land. This Ekrarnama deed is a Khai Khalashi deed under section 95(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and after promulgation of President Order No.88 of 72 and 136 of 72 land automatically redempt and plaintiff has been possessing the land. It was further stated in the plaint that the plaintiff asked the defendant to execute the return kabala in favour of the plaintiff, but the defendant refused to execute the return kabala finally on 24 Agrahaon, 1412 BS corresponding to 12-12-2005. Thus the plaintiff was constrained to file the present suit.

4. The sole defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter-alia, that the plaintiff sold away '20 decimals of land by registered kabala dated 27-3-1967 and on the same day a deed of reconveyance was executed and registered on 1374 BS for a period of four years and it was stipulated in the reconveyance deed that if the plaintiff refund the kabala value Taka 400 (Four hundred) only, in that case defendant will retransfer the said land but the plaintiff will not get benefit of the President's Order No. 88 of 72 and 136 of 72 and the plaintiff is not entitled to get a decree for redemption of the suit land. With these averments the defendant prayed for dismissal of the suit.

5. Both the plaintiff and defendant examined one witness each in their favour to prove their respective case and filed certain documents which was marked as exhibits.

6. The learned trial court after consi-dering the evidence and materials on record decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff by judgment and decree dated 22-4-2009. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree, the defendant preferred Title Appeal No. 92 of 2009 in the Court of District Judge, Patuakhali which subsequently on transfer heard and disposed of by the learned Joint district Judge, Third Court, Patuakhali and the learned Joint District Judge without considering the facts and circumstances of the case allowed the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree of the trial court by the judgment and decree dated 8-11-2010.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with aforesaid judgment and decree dated 8-11-2010 the plaintiff moved this court under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule and Stay.

8. Mr Mohammad Eunus, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioner submits that admittedly the plaintiff Zabed Ali Howlader transfer 20 decimals of land to defendant Amzad Hossain by registered kabala dated 27-3-1967 and on the same day registered Ekra nama was executed between the parties and in such situation the deed executed by the defendant was become a kot mortgage/ Khai Khalashi and the entire consideration for the mortgage was specified by usufructuary of the land during the period of four years but the court of appeal committed gross error of law in not considering such vital aspect of this suit. He further submits that the appellate court failed to consider that the transaction under Exhibit-ka is a mortgage deed and not a sale deed and same was executed with a consideration to reconvey the kabala land by Agreement for reconveyance (Exhibit-1) as such, the appellate court totally misconstrue and misconceived the decision reported in 52 DLR (AD) 132 and failed to appreciate that once a mortgage always a mortgage and bar of past and closed transaction will not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case and thus committed gross error of law.

9. He also submits that the terms of the deed agreement for reconveyance (Exhibit-1) is kot/ Khai Khalashi, but the court of appeal below erroneously found that the transaction was out and out sale erroneously allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In support of his submission Mr Mohammad Eunus relied upon the decision reported in 34 DLR (AD) 237.

10. On the other hand Mr Md Borhan Uddin, the learned Advocate on behalf of the defendant-opposite party contested this revisional application by filing affidavit-in-opposition. The main contention is that since seller plaintiff did not pay the money within 4 years that is within 27-3-1971 from the date of execution of the sale deed, so the transaction will be treated as past and closed and the sale which was made by the plaintiff on 27-3-1967 will treated as out and out sale and the same became absolute. He further submits that since the sale has already became absolute, the present suit of redemption is not maintainable as per President's Order No.88 and 136 of 1972. He also submits that plaintiff has no locus-standi since he miserably failed to pay the money to the buyer-defendant No.1 as per terms stipulated in the Ekrarnama as such right of redemption is not established in favour of the seller. Moreover, since the sale has become absolute on 25-3-1971 long before the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 and 136 of 1972 the conditions of usufructuary mortgage shall not be applicable in the present case.

11. He strenuously argued that since no payment having been made within the stipulated period of Four years, the transaction of sale became absolute as such, the plaintiff was not entitled to get any decree for redemption or reconveyance. In support of his submissions he cited the decisions reported in 26 DLR 394, 52 DLR (AD) 132, 58 DLR (AD) 79 and 1 BLC (AD) (1996) 90. It transpires that there is no dispute in respect of the sale deed dated 27-3-1967 (Exhibit-A) and the Ekrarnama dated 23-3-1967 (Exhibit-1) which was for a period of four years. It is also not disputed that the present suit was filed by the plaintiff Zabed Ali Howlader on 9-4-2006.

12. It appears that the trial court after considering the evidence and materials on record held that the transaction was a complete usufructuary mortgage and the consideration of which was already specified by the usufruct of the land and since the suit was for redemption of mortgage which was filed within specific period of limitation that is within 60 years and on such finding decreed the suit for redemption and on the other hand on the learned judge of the appellate court held that the transaction was out and out sale and said to be treated as past and closed. It was also found by the appellate court that the seller did not pay the money within the period of four years that is 27-7-1971 when the period of Ekrarnama was expired as such the transaction will be treated as past and closed and the deed will not come within the preview of President's Order No. 88 of 1972. In this respect the appellate court relied on the decision of 32 DLR (AD) 233 but it appears that the appellate court totally misconstrue the decision reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233. The appellate court on consideration of the record erroneously found that the present suit is not a mortgage suit as such according to the version of the plaint, the sale deed cannot be treated a deed under section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as such same cannot be treated as kot mortgage/Khai Khalashi under President's Order No. 88 of 1972, 136 of 1972 and 34 of 1973 past and closed matter. The appellate court failed to appreciate that the plaintiff filed the present suit for redemption of the mortgage, but the appellate court failed to appreciate and totally misconstrue the decision reported in 52 DLR (AD) 132 and on such erroneous finding dismissed the suit.

13. It further appears that the court of appeal below failed to appreciate that the plaintiff deposited the consideration money Taka 400 on 3-8-2009 after a delay of 75 days. But the court of appeal below erroneously found that the trial court had no jurisdiction to accept the money on 3-8-2009 long after the period fixed in the judgment passed by the trial court, completely overlooking and in not consideration the specific provision of section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure, wherein it was stated that the court may in its discretion, from time to time, enlarge such period, even though the period originally fixed or granted may have expired.

14. On perusal of the judgment both the courts below it is found that the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant that the opposite party herein confused between the period of subsistence of a usufructuary mortgage and the period of limitation in the case of a suit for redemption of a mortgaged land.

<u>15. Before I entering into the merit of the present case let us look into the provision of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Briefly, SAT Act, 1950). Before the amendment made in the year 1969 by the Ordinance No. XX1 of 1969 in section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act maximum period for a usufructuary mortgage was 15 years and by this amendment the same period was reduced to seven years. And unless earlier redeemed by repayment of the consideration a mortgagor acquires right to redemption on the expiry of the maximum period of seven years, and if the mortgagee does not voluntarily restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, the latter may file a suit for redemption within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of his right of redemption under Article 147 of the Limitation Act. In the present case the suit was filed on 9-4-2006 after expiry of 35 years which is well within the period of limitation and same it is not barred by limitation.</u>

<u>16. Again section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 has been amended by the President's Order No. 88 of 1972 with effect from 3-8-1972, but this amendment did not touch the period of a usufructuary mortgage which is still 7 (seven) years, nor did it affect the period of limitation for redemption suit which is 60 years. Thus it shows that firstly if, on the expiry of the period of a mortgage, the mortgagee does not restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, then the Sub-divisional Magistrate shall on an application by the mortgagor, restore possession of the mortgagor by evicting the mortgagee. In other words, for getting back possession of a mortgaged land the mortgagor need no file any redemption suit, but may get quick remedy by an application to the Sub-divisional Magistrate. The other provision in the amendment is that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law in force, any transfer of land by an out and out sale with a condition for reconveyance shall be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 (seven) years on the expiry of which the mortgagor may get back possession by an application to the Sub-divisional Magistrate. But since transfer as I have found a mortgage, no question arises whether it should be treated as mortgage.</u>

17. It appears from the record of the present case that the sale deed No. 2431 dated 25-3-1967 (Exhibit-A) and four expired on 27-3-1971. President's Order No. 88 of 1972 (Shortly, PO No. 88 of 1972) came into operation on 3-8-1972. Thus it appears that prior to the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 the period of mortgage expired on 27-3-1971. The learned appellate judge wrongly held that the mortgage money was to be paid on or before 27-3-1971 and held that on condition ceased to be operative after promulgation' of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 and 136 of 1972 and amendment of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Mr Md Borhan Uddin, learned Advocate for the opposite-party vehemently argued that section 58C of the Transfer of Property Act will be apply.

18. It further appears that the learned Judge of the appellate court failed to consider that the filing of the suit for redemption of mortgage in a civil court is wholly different from filing of an application under President's Order No. 88 of 1972 before the Revenue "Authority. I fail to understand how the learned judge of the appellate court could hold this in an independent civil suit for redemption of mortgage and opined that the suit is not maintainable. These are two independent proceedings. The reference of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 is totally irrelevant for the purpose of the suit and the learned judge of the appellate court totally misconceived the law governing the suit for redemption of mortgage and most illegally reversed the judgment of the trial court.

<u>19. Before parting with the case it may be mentioned that the learned judge of the appellate court took note of the case of Bangladesh vs Haji Abdul Gani Biswas, reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233. The reference of that case in the contention of the present case is wholly irrelevant. The historical background of the legislation is mentioned in PO No. 88 of 1972 in respect of subsisting usufractuary mortgage is hit by section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is meant to protect the helpless raiyat. A raiyat in Bangladesh cannot interfere into any form of usufractuary mortgage other than complete usufractuary mortgage which is capable of enjoyment for a maximum period of seven years and the raiyat will get back his property under section 95 of SAT Act, 1950.</u>

<u>20. In this connection the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party although submits on this point, but totally misconceived the respective provision of section 95A and PO No. 88 of 1972. I am afraid that the reference of this case shows total non-application of judicial mind of the learned judge of the appellate court. In this respect in the aforesaid cited case reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233 President's Order No. 88 of 1972, President's Order No. 136 of 1972 and President's Order No. 24 of 1973 amending to provision of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and inserting provision of section 95A therein came up for consideration. In that case it was held amongst others "as for the transaction which are not alive before the promulgation of PO No. 88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions past and closed." That conclusion was arrived at in view of the contention that an application for restoration of possession of the mortgage land in respect of transaction past and closed was not maintainable. President's Order No. 88 of 1972 created special forum for restoration of mortgaged property. But it did not take away right of redemption available to a mortgagor by filing a mortgage suit under Order XXXIV of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that view of the matter the submission made by the learned Advocate for the opposite party to that effect is totally erroneous and the view taken by the learned judge of the appellate court are also equally wrong to hold that the suit was not maintainable as the transaction was past and closed.</u>

21. Mr Borhan Uddin, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party cited some decisions reported in (1) 26 DLR 394, (2) 1 BLC (AD) 90, (3) 52 DLR (AD) /32 and (4) 58 DLR (AD) 79. I have carefully gone through the decisions, but those decisions have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case as I have already quoted above.

22. Upon consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant provision of law and decision of our apex court, I find merit in this Rule.

23. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned appellate court is hereby set aside and those of the trial court are restored.

24. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby vacated.

Send down the Lower Court records expeditiously.

End.

caseno: Trade Mark Appeal Nos.1 and 2 of 2014.
lawyer:
Gazi Md. Neamat Hossain, Advocate-------For the Appellants in both the appeals. 
M Hashmat ullah Sheikh, Advocate-------For the Respondent No. 2 in both the appeals.
parties:
Anwar Hossain (Md) Proprietor of M/s Pride Knit Wear Ltd-------Appellants in both the appeals
Vs
Registrar, Patents, Designs and Trade Mark, Dhaka and another--------Respondents in both the appeals
full_judgment:
SM Maniruzzaman J: Since, similar question of law and facts are involved in both the appeals preferred by the respective contending parties as such, both have been taken up for hearing together and are being disposed of by this single judgment.

2. Both the appeals have been preferred challenging the order and decision dated 3-3-2013 passed by the respondent No. 1, Registrar, Patents, Designs and Trade Mark, Dhaka in Opposition Case Nos. 2727 of 2011 and 2845 of 2012 allowing Opposition Case No. 2727 of 2011 and thereby refused to register connected trade mark application bearing No. MP 101364 in Class-25 filed by the appellant and dismissed Opposition Case No. 2845 of 2012 and thereby allowing the connected trade mark application No. 91718 in Class-25 filed by the respondent No. 2.

3. Facts, relevant for disposal of both the appeals, in short, are that the appellant is a renowned business man and is engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling superior quality of socks under the name and style "Pride Knit Wear and MB Hosiery". The appellant has adopted the word "HAZARD" along with special carrier, designs and getup as his trade mark in respect of socks and has been marketing "HAZARD" branded socks all over the country through his dealers, whole sellers and retailers since 2005. It has been contended that the mark "HAZARD" is being continuously used by the appellant under the said trading style and Pride Knit Wear MB Hosiery without any objection from any quarter whatsoever including the respondent No. 2 due to the superior quality of socks being manufactured and sold by the appellant. 14. Section 8(ga) provides that the Registrar cannot accept any mark or part of mark for registration if the said mark can be registered which consists of or contents any scandalize design, or any matter use for fraud. Section 10 provides prohibition of registration of identical or similar trade mark. Sub-section (1) of section 10 provides that no trade mark shall be registered in respect of any goods or description of goods which is identical with a trade mark belonging to a different proprietors and either already on the register in respect of the same goods or description of goods or which so nearly resembles such trade mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion.

15. In the instance cases, the respondent No.2 is the sole user of the mark "HAZARD" and with the said trade mark he has been manufacturing hosiery and garments (including socks) items since 1999. In support of said contention he submitted challan/invoices (Annexure-C16) showing different dates from 6-6-2006-26-6-2006 for supplying "HAZARD" branded items in the local market and also submitted affidavits swearing by the some purchasers/distributors (Annexure-D series) confirming that the respondent M/s Mack Knit Wear are using mark "HAZARD" since 1999. On the other hand the appellant submitted challan/invoices dated 11-12-2006 to 7-12-2009 (Annexure-B) in support of manufacturing and selling socks using the mark "HAZARD" since 2006.

16. Vide the said challan/invoices (Annexure-B) it appears that the appellant manufactured and supplied socks in the local market with trademarks Swan, Addidas and Super Dock. So, it is evidenced by the Annexure-B that excepting mark "HAZARD", the appellant has been manufacturing and supplying Swan, Addidas and Super Dock branded socks in the local market. On the other hand, the opponent respondent has been manufacturing and supplying garments and hosiery (including socks) under the trade mark "HAZARD". It also appears that the respondent's application for registration was prior to the application of the appellant. More so, the respondent has been manufacturing and supplying garments and hosiery (including socks) under the trade mark "HAZARD" since 1999; whereas, the appellant has been manufacturing and supplying socks with trade mark "HAZARD" since 2006. The Registrar, however, allowed the respondent objection holding, inter alia—

“M/s Mack Knit Wear “HAZARD” মার্কটির ব্যবহার ১৯৯৯ লাল থেকে এবং M/s Pride Knit Wear এর Hazard মার্ক এর ব্যবহার ২০০৬ সাল থেকে এতে প্রমাণিত হয় M/s Mack Knit Wear “HAZARD” মার্কটির prior user এবং Trademarks Act, 2009 এর ৮(গ) ধারা অনুযায়ী ট্রাইব্যুনালের নিকট প্রতীয়মান হয়েছে যে একই মার্ক একই ক্ষেত্রে দুইজনকে দেয়া হলে বাজারে বিভ্রান্তির সৃষ্টি হবে।”

17. Another assertion of the appellant is that the respondent objection case is barred by the principle of estoppel. Conversely, the opponent respondent submits that as per his tender the appellant supplied "HAZARD" branded socks for the time being to fill up the backward linkage. In this regard, we have noticed from Annexure-B series that the appellant supplied "HAZARD" branded socks to the opponent respondent several times but, he included trademarks Swan, Addidas and Super Dock in his challan/invoices. However, he did not include mark "HAZARD" therein. As such, the appellant cannot claim that he has been manufacturing and supplying socks under the trade mark "HAZARD". In addition, the appellant could not place any agreement before the Registrar in support of allowing him to manufacture and supply "HAZARD" branded socks in the market by the present respondent. As such, the contention so has been raised to that effect falls through.

18. On perusal of the relevant provisions of law regarding registration of trade mark, it appears that when nearly resembled trade mark is claimed by different proprietors, the Registrar as per provision under section 10(2) of the Act, 2009 may give registration to different proprietors considering the trade mark being used concurrently and with honest purpose. In the instant appeals both the parties filed objection cases against each other. However, if the Registrar would allow registration of trade mark "HAZARD" for supplying and manufacturing socks to the appellant, he would not use mark "HAZARD" honest purpose since, the appellant is using other 3(three) trade marks for manufacturing socks. Besides, from the logo of the mark "HAZARD" in both the applications, we found that those are visually and phonetically identical i.e. "" not nearly resemble. Hence, section 10(2) of the Act does not allow to give registration of identical trade mark to different proprietors, although the mark is to be used concurrently and with honest purpose.

19. The issue involves in the instant appeals has been discussed by the Apex Court in the several judgments of our jurisdiction as well as Indian jurisdiction.

20. In the case of Abdul Motaleb vs Haji Aftab Minh, reported in 16 BLT 138, it has been held that—

"The respondent No. 1 is using the Trade Mark "Bonoful" illegally and therefore the claim of use of the Trade Mark "Bonoful" for over 14 years by the respondent hereof has no legal value and said period cannot be counted for the purpose of section 10(2) of the Trade Mark Act to get benefit as honest concurrent user and hence granting of registration of Trade Mark "Bonoful" in favour of Respondent No. 2 under section 10(2) of the Trademarks Act is illegal."

21. In the case of Nabisco Biscuit and Bread Factory Limited, Dhaka, Appellant vs Baby Food products Limited, Dhaka Respondent reported in 28 BLD 304, it has been held that—

"Section 8 of the Act prohibits, inter alia, registration of any trade mark which is likely to deceive or cause confusion or otherwise be disentitled to protection in a Court of justice. Section 10 of the Act further prohibits, inter alia, registration of any trade mark which is identical with a trade mark belonging to a different proprietor and either already on the register in respect of same goods or description of goods or which so nearly resemble such trade mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion."

22. In the case of MK Electric Limited, Shrubbery Road, Edmonton, London N9 OPB (UK), appellant, vs Md. Mozammel Hoque, Trading as MK Electric Industries, Respondents reported in 27 BLD 445, it has been held that—

"There is a legal prohibition for registration if a trade mark which is phonetically identical with the previously registered trade mark. In such circumstances the Registrar has to record a finding of fact on the materials before him, if he comes to the conclusion that the matter falls within the prohibited category then he has no discretion but has to refuse Registration."

23. In the case of Tosiba Appliances Company-Opponent vs Kabushiki Kaisha Toshiba-Applicant in 2002 (24) PTC 654 (Reg.) (at page 655, 5th line from top) it has been held that—

"The honest concurrent use is the main element to be considered by the Tribunal for allowing a trade mark to proceed for concurrent registration under section 12(3) of the Act. The honesty of the use of a trade mark has to be considered from the commercial point of view. The honesty or dishonesty of use of a trade mark relates back to its adoption. If a trade mark had been adopted honestly is subsequent use has to be honest. But to the contrary, if a trade mark had been dishonestly adopted its subsequent use of any length of time cannot launder the vice of dishonesty of adoption. If a person adopts a trade mark having knowledge of an earlier existing identical or deceptively similar trade mark, such adoption has to be dishonest adoption is tainted with mala fide intention of the person who adopts such trade mark."

24. In the case of SM Taufiq vs National Biscuit Co., New York, reported in PLD 1962 (WP) Karachi 355 (from 4th line of page No. 359), it has been held that—

"The evidence produced by the respondents undoubtedly proves that after 1940, in the territories now comprising Pakistan, the trade mark "Nabisco" was neither used nor had any reputation till 1947, or after partition up to the time they filed application for the registration of the said trade mark." Therefore, it is found that the appellants SM Taufiq and others being the prior user, the appeal was allowed and got registration for Trade Mark "Nabisco".

<u>25. Considering of the above context, it is discovered that section 8 of the Act, 2009 prohibits registration of any trade mark or part of the mark which is likely to deceive or cause confusion and or any matter use for fraud and or otherwise be disentitled in a Court of justice. Section 10 of Act, 2009 further prohibits registration of any trade mark which is identical with a trade mark belonging to a different proprietor and either already on the register in respect of same goods or description of goods or which so likely to deceive or cause confusion. In the instant appeals, both the contending parties filed applications for registration of trade mark "HAZARD" for supplying hosiery/garments/socks in the local market and both marks are phonetically and visually identical. However, sections 8 and 10(1) prohibit registration identical marks in respect of same goods or description of goods to different persons.</u>

26. Moreover, the respondent is the prior user of trade mark "HAZARD" and his application was filed prior to the application of the appellant. The Registrar considering the said facts and the provisions of law granted registration of trade mark "HAZARD" in favour of the present respondent.

27. In view of the above facts and circumstances of the cases, findings and observations we find no legal infirmity in the impugned order and decision so passed by the Registrar refusing to register the trade mark "HAZARD" in favour of the appellant.

28. In the result, both the appeals are dismissed without any order as to costs.

29. The impugned order and decision dated 3-3-2013 passed by the respondent No. 1, Registrar, Patents, Designs and Trademarks, Dhaka in Opposition Case Nos. 2727 of 2011 and 2845 of 2012 allowing Opposition Case No. 2727 of 2011 and thereby refused to register connected trade mark application bearing No. MP 101364 in Class-25 filed by the appellant and dismissed Opposition Case No. 2845 of 2012 and thereby allowing the connected trade mark application No. 91718 in Class-25 filed by the respondent No. 2 is hereby upheld.

30. Communicate the judgment and order to the concerned respondents forthwith.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Md Mehedi Hasan Chowdhury with Apurbo Kumar Biswas, Advocates-------For the Petitioners. 
Tanjib-ul Alam with Kazi Ershadul Alarm, Advocates--------For the Respondents Nos. 2-4.
parties:
Dr Ahmed Abu Saleh and others--------Petitioners
Vs
Government of Bangladesh represented by its Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and others---------Respondents
full_judgment:
JBM Hassan J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned office order bearing No. BSMMU/2018/8911 dated 7-8-2018 (Annexure-A to the writ petition) signed by the respondent No. 3 imposing restrictions in distributing "User Fees" amongst the doctors, technologists and other staff of the concerned departments of the Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University should not be declared to have been issued without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Relevant facts leading to issuance of the Rule Nisi are that the petitioners No. 1-5 are the teachers of the Basic Science Faculty of the Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University (the University) being Professors, Departments of Microbiology, Biochemistry and Molecular Biology and Virology. Petitioners No. 6 and 7 are the Chief Medical Technologists of the department of Biochemistry and Microbiology respectively of the said University. The University was established by the Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University Ain, 1998 (the University Act, 1998).

3. Since 1937, hospitals of Indian subcontinent have been collecting "User Fees" which is still a common practice in India, Pakistan and Srilanka. The East Pakistan government also approved the collection of 'User Fees' and distribution of the same as evident from the memo No. 2132-Medi dated Dacca, the 15th June, 1954. After independence of Bangladesh, the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare also permitted the practice of collection and distribution of 'User Fees' (50% will be disbursed amongst doctors, technologists and other staff of the concerned departments) vide memo No. MEH/1M-15/83/788 dated 5-2-1984 and memo No. M E H /1M-15 /15 dated 17-4-1985.

4. After establishment of the University by the “বঙ্গবন্ধু শেখ মুজিব মেডিক্যাল বিশ্ববিদ্যালয় আইন, ১৯৯৮” (the Act, 1998), the University issued an office order on 27-12-1998 stating that 40% of the 'User Fees' of various examinations would be disbursed amongst the doctors, technologists and other staff of the concerned departments of the University. Subsequently, reducing the ratio rate the University issued another memo on 24-3-1999 under the signature of the Registrar stating that 30% of the "User Fees" of various examinations would be disbursed amongst the doctors, technologists and other staff of the concerned departments of the University and it has been continuing.

5. All of a sudden, on 7-8-2018 the Registrar of the University issued the impugned memo baring No. বিএসএমএমইউ/২০১৮/৮৯১১ dated 7-8-2018 to the effect that 30% of the "User Fees" of various examinations would be disbursed amongst the doctors, technologists and other staff of the concerned department of the University but they will not receive "User Fees" beyond their respective two basic pay rolls. Further, out of those 30%, 10% would be deposited in the Central Fund of the University for distribution amongst employees of other departments of the University. The petitioners have challenged this memo and obtained the present Rule.

6. The University as respondents No. 2-4 appearing in the Rule Nisi has filed an affidavit-in-opposition controverting the statements of the writ petition. Contentions of these respondents, inter-alia, are that the Syndicate of the University by its 70th meeting held on 12-6-2018 took decision regarding distribution of "User Fees" amongst its teachers and employees in a certain manner keeping in mind about the best interest of the employees of the University. Pursuant to said decision the impugned order has been passed. It is further stated that departments of Radiology, Pathology, Microbiology, Biometrics and other similar departments receive multiple additional allowances apart from their basic salary. Whereas there are some departments which do not have additional source of earning. In order to remove such discrepancies in earning of allowances, the University commissioned a Committee to recommend how to best distribute the "User Fees" among all employees of the University.

7. In exercise of statutory power and authority incorporated in the University Act, 1998, the University took similar decision in the past on 27-12-1998 and 24-3-1999 which were never challenged by anyone.

8. It is further contended that the memo dated 5-2-1984 and memo dated 17-4-1985 (Annexure-C and C/1 to the writ petition) are not applicable relating to the University since those memos were issued with respect to the Government hospitals and institutions whereas the instant respondent is an autonomous body and it is governed by the Act, 1998 and on the similar proposition of law the Rule 24 of “নিরাপদ রক্ত সঞ্চালন বিধিমালা, ২০০৮” is not applicable relating to the University.

9. By filing supplementary-affidavit the writ petitioners further state that the Doctors, Technicians and other staff of the petitioners' departments are working from 8-30 am to 8-00 pm and in addition emergency test services are also open for 24 hours and even public holidays doctors, technicians and other staff do perform duties by way of rotations. At the time of establishment of the said University under the University Act, 1998, all the doctors, technicians and other officials were ensured that the service benefits and allowances under the Government rules will be followed in the said University. The Syndicate of the University has no authority to determine "User Fees" of the petitioners without taking any recommendation of the Finance Committee or approval from the concerned committee. Despite with an ulterior motive imposed restrictions in respect of "User Fees" distributed upon the petitioners. Furthermore, during 70th Syndicate Meeting, one of the Syndicate member of the said University made misstatement to other members stating that Appellate Division ordered that the teachers of the University would not receive any "User Fees", although the Appellate Division did not pass any such order.

10. It is also stated that in comparison to other departments risk factor of infections and others diseases of doctors, technicians and other staff of Microbiology, Molecular Biology, Virology, Biochemistry and other related departments of the University are higher. The doctors, technicians and other officials of the Department of Cardiology and Anaesthesia Department of the University are receiving 35% and 30% of the "User Fees" respectively.

11. On several occasions, Microbiology, Molecular Biology, Virology, Biochemistry and other related departments of the University have been earning a huge amount of money and transferring the same to the central account of the University and thus these departments are contributing to develop the University by earning revenue. The concerned departments of the University are also providing free service to the patients (including freedom fighters) who are unable to pay any fees and that the price rate of the tests are cheap in comparison with private clinical Laboratories.

12. Human Rights and Peace for Bangladesh filed writ petition No. 9587 of 2010 before the High Court Division wherein a direction was given on 19-2-2012 upon the authorities to stop collection of "User Fees" at the Government Hospitals. But operation of the said order was stayed by order dated 23-10-2012 of the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal (CPLA) No. 2616 of 2012. One Md. Sirajul Islam, Medical Technologist of the Dhaka Medical College Hospital also filed writ petition No. 7299 of 2013 before the High Court Division challenging the impugned office order dated 14-7-2014 issued by the Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Health and Welfare Affairs restraining the authorities from disbursing "User Fees" amongst the doctors, technicians and other concerned officials of the Government Hospitals. Thereafter, on 23-7-2013 the High Court Division was pleased to stay operation of the aforesaid impugned office order dated 14-7-2014 and also directed the respondents to disburse "User Fees" amongst the doctors, technicians and other concerned officials. Subsequently, challenging the aforesaid order, Co-Ordination Committee of Clinical Societies and others filed the CPLA (Civil Petition) No. 1987 of 2013 before the Appellate Division and but on 7-12-2014 the Appellate Division dismissed the said Civil Petition.

13. The respondents No. 2-4 have also filed supplementary affidavit-in-opposition denying the statements of the supplementary affidavit of the petitioners contending, infer alia, are that the petitioners do not work from 8-30 am to 8-00 pm each day and it is also not possible to work in such a manner at a stretch and that although the petitioners are claiming to be working 24 hours at the emergency lab, no reports are delivered on emergency basis to the patients from these departments. CCU, ICU and Emergency Departments have their separate lab facilities from where emergency reports are delivered to the emergency patients and doctors and that technologists and other employees of these departments and their labs do not get any part of the fees for the services they provide.

14. It is further contended that nowhere in the University Act, 1998 it is provided that the Syndicate is required to take approval from the Finance Committee for making policy to distribute "User Fees". The office orders upon which the petitioners are relying on, have not been approved either by the Syndicate or recommended by the Finance Committee. As such, according to the argument of the petitioners they do not have authority to get any "User Fees" in the first place inasmuch as the office orders giving rise to their legal rights of receiving "User Fees" are illegal and the petitioners are liable for repaying the amount that they have received in the name of "User Fees" which have been distributed by the concerned departments among themselves without any consultation or recommendation or approval from the University authority.

15. It is further contended that none of the petitioners come in close contact to any of the samples received by the lab. Samples are received by the phlebotomists who work in the University on a daily basis and thereby they do not receive any part of the "User Fees". Then the samples goes to lab where the technologists put the sample into machines following Standard Operating Procedure. Thereafter, the machines generate data after analyzing the samples which are being forwarded for preparation of reports. After preparation of the reports those are sent to relevant doctors for signatures. As such, there is no steps involved wherein the petitioners come to close contract of any samples and hence question of risk of petitioners does not arise. In fact, the petitioners are working in the safer environment than the other departments inasmuch as they do not come in close contact with any patients with contagious disease, on the other hand, the other doctors, nurses, medical attendants etc. come to close contact with patients with contagious disease e.g patients with Nipah virus, AIDS, tuberculosis etc.

16. According to section 48 of the University Act, 1998 all these fees and charges collected by these departments belong to the University and must be deposited in the central fund. But, the petitioners' departments are treating these money as their own fund. In the internal audit of four departments being Microbiology, Pathology, Biochemistry and Virology revealed that the teachers, doctors and employees of these departments took Taka 8,09,27,429 in excess. Furthermore, some of the departments without any consultation or approval from the Syndicate or Administrative wing or Finance Committee kept the money in fixed deposit as if these are their own funds. As a result, the University had to ask for return of the money. Even after that, they did not return the full money.

17. It is further contended that the departments are not providing free service. It is the University which provides free service, not the petitioners or their departments. All the employees of these departments receive salary for their service in the University. In addition to that, they distribute a large amount of money, about 10 times of their basic salary, on account of "User Fees" even though they are getting paid for such services. Further, the University pays for the establishment, development and maintenance of infrastructure, reagents used for testing purpose and other ancillary costs associated with the tests using which the petitioners and their departments provide services. The University prepared a statement showing total income and the excess amount received by the teachers, doctors and other employees of the these departments from which it appears that in the last 12 years, they have received more than Taka 75 crore in excess in violation of the decision taken in 25th Syndicate meeting dated 27-5-2007. The audit report of the Biochemistry Department for the year 2017-2018 shows that in this year, the professors of this department received around Taka 5,25,888 per month which is about 7-10 times of their basic salary that are drawn by them from the University.

18. By filing another supplementary affidavit-in-opposition the University respondents further contend that the concerned departments purchase their respective reagents and other consumable items for conducting tests. The costs of these consumable and other items are being paid from the University fund of 70% and the teachers, doctors and employees of the concerned departments Take 30% without any deduction. The Syndicate of the University in its 25th meeting held on 27-5-2007 decided that 30% of the profit of the income generated from laboratory and other examinations and various operation procedures would be distributed amongst the teachers, doctors, officers and employees. But, the petitioners and their predecessors have been receiving 30% of the income instead of 30% of the profit which effectively means that they have been misappropriating the public fund.

19. The concerned departments fixed the charges for the tests conducted by them without any consultation or recommendation or approval from either the Syndicate or the Finance Committee. It is further stated that the Laboratory Service Management Ordinance does not confer any authority to the departments for fixing the charges for such fees.

20. Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hasan Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has advanced the following submissions:

(i) The petitioners' departments have been enjoying "User Fees" since 1937 and that at the time of issuance of the memo dated 5-2-1984, the University was a government organization and by the said government circular the employees including teachers of the medical college and hospitals were enjoying "User Fees". After establishment of the University by the Act, 1998, pursuant to office order dated 27-12-1998 and 24-3-1999 the "User Fees" are being distributed among the teachers and employees of the concerned departments of the University as per 70-30 ratio.

(ii) Since long the petitioners have been enjoying the 30% of the total "User Fees" but all of a sudden the impugned order was issued referring to the Syndicate decision curtailing the petitioners right reducing the ratio and limiting the total amount entitled to be received.

(iii) The Syndicate cannot take such decision without consultation of the Finance Committee and so the impugned decision has been taken in violation of section 23(2)(Gha) of the Act, 1998.

(iv) According to report of various Organizations including WHO, the nature of duty of the petitioners' departments involve high risk of life and disease and moreover, they have to remain on duty about 8-00 am and so, to 8-00 pm Considering all these aspects the "User Fees" are being distributed amongst the teachers and employees of the concerned departments for a long time. Therefore, the impugned order taking decision to share it by other departments having no connection with such job, is arbitrary and malafide.

(v) Considering similar nature of life risk, the other departments are also sharing the "User Fees" under the University but instead of sharing with those "User Fees" the Syndicate interfered only to the extent of petitioners' departments following pick and choose policy. Therefore, the impugned order is unfair and not reasonable. (vO By the Act, 2002 and the Rules, 2008 the "User Fees" are being shared by the employees and concerned persons in all the Government hospitals. Hence, the petitioners are also entitled being involved with the similar nature of duties under the University.

(vii) Stopping sharing of "User Fees", was challenged in a writ petition by two employees of the concerned departments and that by the interim order the same being stayed, against the interim order one Professor Billal Alam unsuccessfully filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal before the Appellate Division and thereafter out of grudge and malafide intention as Syndicate member he influenced the other members to take the impugned decision and so it is liable to be interfered.

21. In support of aforesaid submissions, the learned Advocate refers to the case of Unique Hotel and Resorts Ltd, vs Bangladesh, reported in 15 BLC 770, SSA Bangladesh Ltd. vs Engineer Mahmud-ul-Islam, reported in 12 BLT (AD) 171 = 9 BLC (AD) 84, FazIur Rahman Chowdhury vs Bangladesh, reported in 39 DLR 314, Agragami Engineers Ltd. vs Bangladesh Bank, reported in 45 DLR 134, Bangladesh vs Md. Abul Hossain, reported in 23 BLD (AD) 129.

22. On the other hand, Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents No.2-4 contends as follows:

(i) Sharing of "User Fees" by the teachers and employees of the concerned departments has never been sanctioned under any law of the University and although the teachers and staff of the concerned departments have been receiving the same since long but no amount of consent will give legitimacy to an action which is otherwise illegal and does not have any legal sanction, in other words, the practice of distribution of "User Fees" is not in accordance with the Act, 1998 and so the petitioner cannot take advantage of such long practice as to sharing of "User Fees". In support of his submission, Mr. Alam refers to the case of Chairman, Rajdhani, Unnayan Katripakkha (RAJUK) vs A Rouf Chowdhury, reported in 61 DLR (AD) 28.
