full_judgment:
Zubayer Rahman Chowdhury, J : The issuance of a letter dated 16-6-2014 by respondent No. 2 cancelling the panel prepared for appointment of Nikah Registrar in Ward Nos. 7, 8, 9 of Pourashava and Upazilla Fulbari in the District of Dinajpur has led to the filing of the instant writ petition by the petitioner, whose name appeared at serial number 1 in the said panel. 

2. Briefly stated, facts relevant for disposal of the Rule are that respondent No. 4, by Memo dated 1-4-2012, invited applications for appointment of Nikah Registrar in respect of Ward Nos. 1, 2, 3 (one post) and Ward Nos. 7, 8 and 9 (one post), both under Pourashava and Upazilla Fulbari, District Dinajpur. Upon receiving applications from the prospective candidates, respondent No. 5 prepared a panel of three candidates in respect of Ward Nos. 7, 8 and 9 of Fulbari Poushava, wherein the petitioner's name appeared at serial No. 1, as evident from the Memo dated 8-5-2012. A recommendation was also received by respondent No. 1 from the local Member of Parliament vide Memo dated 10-4-2014 recomMending the appointment of the petitioner. 

3. During the pendency of the process of appointment and prior to finalization of the same, the impugned Memo dated 16-6-2014 was issued Cancelling the panel sent by the Advisory Committee in respect of Ward Nos. 7, 8 and 9 of Fulbari Poushava. At the same time, respondent No. 5 was directed to prepare a fresh panel for appointment in the said Ward. Being aggrieved, the petitioner moved this Court by filing the instant application under Article 102 (2) of the Constitution. 

4. By order dated 16-1-2017, a supplementary Rule was issued in the following terms : 
"Let a Rule Nisi issue calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the office order dated 29-12-2016 contained in Memo N9. Bichar-7/2N-05/93(Part)-747 issued under the signature of the Senior Assistant Secretary, Bichar-7, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Dhaka (Respondent No. 3) appointing Mr Md Sekendor Ali as the Nikah Registrar of the Word Nos. 8 and 9 of Fulbari Pourashova, Fulbari, Dinajpur during pendency of the Writ Petition (Annexure I) should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper." 

5. At the time of issuance of the supplementary Rule, the operation of the order dated 29.12.2016 was stayed for a period of 3 (three) months, which was subsequently extended from time to time. It is to be noted that by order dated 14-2-2017, Md Sekandar Ali was impleaded as respondent No. 6 in the instant writ petition. 

6. Mr Md Humayun Kabir, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the action of the respondents in cancelling the panel is arbitrary and malafide. The learned Advocate submits that the Advisory Committee formed a panel comprising of three candidates, being satisfied as to their qualifications. He submits that once a panel had been prepared by the Advisory Committee and thereafter forwarded to the Ministry, it was incumbent upon the Ministry to grant approval and appoint the petitioner as Nikali Registrar in respect of Ward Nos. 7, 8 and 9, whose name appeared at serial No. 1, in the said panel. He submits that in the absence of any disqualification of the candidates, the respondents had no authority to cancel the panel and take steps to prepare a fresh panel in respect of the very same wards. 

7. Referring to the impugned order itself, as evidenced by Annexure D, the learned Advocate submits that the reasons which have been assigned in the said letter is neither tenable in law nor supported by any Rules, more particularly the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules. He further submits that the reason given by respondent No. 2 for cancelling the panel stands contrary to the provision of the Constitution, which does not allow any discrimination on the ground of gender. 

8. Mr Kabir submits that every citizen of the country has the right to hold a public office, subject to having the requisite qualifications. The learned Advocate submits that there is no document on record to indicate that the petitioner does not hold the requisite qualifications to be appointed as Nikah Registrar. He submits that merely because all the three candidates selected in the panel happen to be females, that cannot be a ground for cancellation of the same. He submits that the conduct of the respondent is not only malafide and arbitrary, but is also violative of the petitioner's right guaranteed under the Constitution. Referring to the decision reported in 2006 (14) BLT (HCD) 33 = 57 DLR 201, he submits that as the issue of gender equality has been reaffirmed by this Court in the aforesaid judgment, the petitioner has a right to be appointed in the post of Nikah Registrar. 

9. The Rule is being opposed by respondent No. 6 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. 

10. Mr Mohiuddin MA Kader, the learned Advocate appearing in opposition to the Rule submits that the impugned order was issued taking into account the nature and scope of the role and function of a Nikah Registrar, which is distinct and separate from that in any other post in the Government service. He submits the primary task of a Nikah Registrar is to conduct and record marriages of Muslims couples. He submits that a Muslim marriage ceremony is essentially a religious ceremony, which is conducted in accordance with religious rites. 

11. Mr Kader submits that more often than not, a marriage ceremony is usually conducted in a mosque and there is no particular time as to when such ceremony is to be held. Elaborating his submission, the learned Advocate submits that the Nikah Registrar of the concerned Ward or Union is required to conduct the marriage ceremony at the venue where the marriage is being held, either at a masjid or a public place or a private residence. Therefore, by the very nature of the job, a Nikah Registrar is required to travel to distant places and sometimes even early in the morning when a marriage ceremony is solemnized after Fazr prayers. 

12. The learned Advocate submits that in the instant case, the panel comprised of three lady candidates. He submits that given the state of communication and the road-network is the rural areas, particularly during the monsoon season and also given the fact that at times, a Nikah Registrar may be required to travel quiet a distance to solemnize a marriage ceremony, which may involve crossing a river or canal by boat, it is not ideal that the Nikah Registrar should be a lady. 

13. The learned Advocate acknowledges that there is no legal bar in appointing a lady as Nikah Registrar. However, according to Mr Kader, the provisions of Rule 6 (Ka) of the Muslim Marriage and Divorce (Registration) Rules 2009, provides that when a vacancy occurs in the post of Nikah Registrar on account of the incumbent's death or retirement, in case of the new appointment, the son of the Nikah Registrar, if he is otherwise qualified, should be given preference. The learned Advocate submits that this particular provision has been made providing for appointment of the son of the Nikah Registrar. He submits that although the daughter has not been expressly excluded, nevertheless, it is implied. He submits that it is because of the practical difficulties and demands of this position, more particularly in a rural area, that the Rule 6 (Ka) provides for appointment of the son, and not the daughter of the incumbent. 

14. We have perused the application and considered the submissions advanced at the Bar. 

15. The issue before this Court raises a question of considerable public interest and importance. The Nikah Registrar is primarily entrusted with the duty to solemnize and record marriages that take place between Muslim couples. A marriage ceremony is not a merely a family or social event, it is essentially a religious ceremony, which entails certain religious functions. The marriage ceremony is usually conducted either by the Nikah Registrar himself or by the Imam of the masjid of the locality where the marriage ceremony takes place. More often than not, a marriage ceremony is held either at the bride's residence or at a public place (Auditorium or Community Hall) or even in a masjid. It requires the presence of at least two witnesses on both sides, who are required to sign the Marriage Register after a marriage is solemnized. 

16. In the instant case, the appointment relates to the office of a Nikah Registrar in a rural area, where obviously the transportation system is not so developed as in the urban areas and therefore, public transport is not readily available. It is also to be noted that marriage ceremonies take place throughout the year and in a country like Bangladesh, where monsoon lasts for several months, it may be quiet difficult for a Nikah Registrar to attend the ceremonies in the rainy season, and that too at night. It may also require the Nikah Registrar to travel some distance to conduct a marriage ceremony, which may also involve crossing a river or canal by boat. These practical difficulties cannot either be taken lightly or be discounted altogether in considering the appointment of a person in the post of Nikah Registrar in a rural area. 

17. The learned Advocate for the petitioner is correct in submitting that the Constitution ensures gender equality. There is no dispute that our Constitution guarantees equality of opportunity and also ensures equality amongst the genders. However, the role and duty of a Nikali Registrar is separate and distinct from any other public office. 

18. As we have observed at the very outset, the primary role and duty of a Nikah Registrar is to solemnize the marriage between Muslim couples, which is essentially a religious ceremony. On account of rapid urbanisation coupled with lack of open space, a recent trend has developed to have the Nikah ceremony solemnized at the local masjid. It has to be borne in mind that due to certain physical condition, a lady cannot enter the mosque during a certain time of the month. She is even excused from performing the mandatory daily prayers during this particular time. This physical disqualification does not allow her to conduct the religious task. We are mindful of the fact that a Muslim marriage is a religious ceremony and has to be guided by the terms and dictates of Islam. 

19. We have perused the decision referred to by Mr Humayun Kabir. While agreeing in principle with regard to exposition of the gender equality clause as enshrined in our Constitution, we hasten to add that in the said reported case the writ petition was filed in relation to the office of a Ward Commissioner. Needless to observe that the office of a Ward Commissioner does not entail any religious function and duty as that of a Nikah Registrar. Therefore, the said decision does not apply to the present case. In our view, the practical difficulty, more particularly in the rural areas of Bangladesh, has necessitated the cancellation of the panel by respondent No. 2. This is not a question of discrimination; rather, it is a question of practical necessity. 

20. Be that as it may, having regard to the somewhat extra-ordinary circumstances of the case, we are inclined to hold that the impugned Memo dated 16-6-2014, passed by respondent No. 2, does not warrant any interference from this Court. 

21. In the result, the Rule is discharged. Consequently, The supplementary Rule, issued on 16-1-2017, also stands discharged. 

22. The order of stay, granted at the time of issuance of the Rule dated 16-1-2017, is hereby recalled and vacated. 

There will be no order as to cost. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md Nazrul Islam Talukder, J : On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the people's Republic of Bangladesh, this Rule Nisi, at the instance of the petitioner, was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the seizure of the petitioner's passport being No.AF5129741 by the Respondent No.3 and thereby debarring the petitioner from going abroad and entering into Bangladesh without having any order of the competent authority or any Court of law and infringing fundamental right of the petitioner as guaranteed under Article 36 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, should not be declared illegal, without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the Respondent Nos.2 and 3 should not be directed to release the petitioner's passport being No.AF5129741 and/or pass such other or further order or orders a s to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. It appears from the record that a Division Bench of High Court Division at the time of issuance of the Rule Nisi directed the Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to release the petitioner's passport being No.AF5129741 within 24(twenty four) hours from the date of receipt of the copy of the order. 

3. It may be noted that being aggrieved by the aforesaid ad-interim order, the Anti-Corruption Commission preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2423 of 2018 before the Appellate Division and on 25-6-2018, the learned Judges of the Appellate Division after hearing the parties directed to continue the order of stay passed by the learned Judge-in-Chamber till disposal of the Rule and the said order runs as under:—
"We have heard the Advocates of both the parties and perused the impugned order of the High Court Division. We are of the view that the ends of justice would be best served, if the Rule itself is disposed of on merit by the High Court Division. 
Let the Rule be heard and disposed of by the High Court Division expeditiously. 
However, the order of stay passed by the learned Judge-in-Chamber be continued till disposal of the Rule. The petition is accordingly disposed of with the above observations and direction." 

4. It is stated in the application that the Anti-Corruption Commission being informant lodged a First Information Report with Motijheel Police Station DMP, Dhaka against the petitioner and some other accused-persons under sections 4(2)/4(3) of the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain, 2012 read with sections 409/420/109 of the Penal Code, 1860 and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, which was registered as Motijheel (DMP) Police Station Case No. 30 dated 25-1-2018. It is alleged in the FIR that on 25-1-2018, one Md Gulshan Anowar, Assistant Director, Head Office of Durnity Daman Commission, Segunbagicha, Ramna, Dhaka lodged a First Information Report (hereinafter referred as FIR) before the Officer-in-Charge of Motijheel Police Station against the petitioner and others under sections 409/420/109 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sections 4(2)14(3) of the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain, 2012 alleging, inter-alia, that during inquiry, perusing and examining the records, it was found that the confessing accused Saiful Haque, that is, the petitioner was known to accused Kurram Abdullah, Abdus Samad Khan and M. Wahidul Haque, Chairman of AB Bank. 

5. On that advantage and in order to mis-appropriate and launder money, the present petitioner managed and introduced the members of fraudulent syndicate with the Chairman of AB Bank and held several meetings with them in Dubai and Bangladesh. Accused M Wahidul Haque and Abu Hena Mostafa Kamal beyond the knowledge of AB Bank went to Dubai and formed two companies-one in Singapore namely Pinacol Global Fund (PGF) and another in Dubai namely Cheng Bao General Trading LLC being Account No.AE-8000-3001-0094-5191-2400-1. Subsequently, M. Wahidul Haque and Abu Hena Mostafa Kamal at their own initiative, executed a draft agreement with the members of fraudulent syndicate, placed the same before the Bank and the Board of Directors approved the same with some conditions that after releasing 60 Million US Dollar from PGF, AB Bank would give guarantee of 20 Million US Dollar and the account would be operated under joint 'signature following the approval to be taken from the Bangladesh Bank. 

6. It has been further stated that before final execution, the agreement has to be placed before the Board of Bank but the accused M. Wahidul Haque, Abu Hena Mostafa Karnal and FazItir Rahman with a malafide intention breaching the trust and abusing the power very technically omitted the word of Bank guarantee and the final deed of agreement was executed under the signature of M. Wahidul Haque, the then Chairman and Md Fazlur Rahman, the then Managing Director. Subsequently they took signature of the representative of so-called Pinacol Global Fund (PGF) without the particulars and addresses of those people. It has been further mentioned that for authorized signature of the account, the PGF would arrange residence VISA in. Dubai for M. Wahidul Haque but accused M. Wahidul Haque and accused Abu Hena Mostafa Kamal without getting any residence VISA went to Dubai on 07-2-2014 and stayed there till 09-2-2014. During their stay in Dubai, without opening Account under joint signature as per deed of agreement, they opened account with ADCB Bank and directed the concerned officers of AB Bank to release 20 Million US Dollar to the Account No. AE 8003-0010-0945-1912-4001 opened in the Bank of ADCB in Dubai. Due to pressure and instruction by the accused, the Bank officials passed the relevant orders and accordingly, through 3 swift transactions, accused Shamim Ahmed Chowdhury, Abu Hena Mostafa Kamal, Md Mahfuzul Islam, Md Nurul Azim and Lockman without legal sanction violating condition of agreement transmitted the above mentioned 20 Million US Dollar. It has been further stated that after transmitting the above mentioned 20 Million US Dollar, the account in abroad and the company at Singapore were closed and the existence of Bank Account and the company in abroad was not found after transmitting money. 

7. By the aforesaid means and ways, all the accused including the present petitioner out of criminal conspiracy abusing their power and authority resorting to fraudulent activities laundered and transferred 20 million US dollar to Dubai from AB Bank Ltd through corruption and suspicious transactions, which being money laundering offences are punishable offences under sections 409/420/109 of the Penal Code, section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 read with section 4(2)(3) of the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain, 2012. Hence, the FIR. 

8. The further statements made in the application by the petitioner are as follows:—
a. That the petitioner was arrested in connection with the aforesaid case and he was produced before the Court of learned Chief Metropolitan magistrate, Dhaka vide police forwarding dated 25-1-2018 with a prayer for remand of the petitioner for a period of 10 (ten) days. 
b. That the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka was pleased to allow 3 (three) days remand of the petitioner vide order dated 25-1-2018; after completion of police remand, the petitioner was again produced before the learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka vide forwarding dated 30-1-2018.
c. That on 7-1-02018, the petitioner was directed by the Respondent No. 3 to appear before his office. Accordingly, the petitioner appeared before the Respondent No. 3 and he was interrogated by the Respondent No. 3 elaborately; at one stage, the Respondent No. 3 directed the petitioner for depositing his passport forthwith to him, otherwise he would be arrested in connection with the case. In that circumstance, the petitioner deposited his passport to the Respondent No. 3, but the Respondent No. 3 did not give any deposit slip or paper to the petitioner in connection therewith. 

9. The. Respondent No. 2, the Anti-Corruption Commission represented by its Chairman, has submitted affidavit-in-Opposition controverting the statements and grounds taken in the application and categorically stated that the statements and grounds are vague, incorrect, misconceived, misleading, baseless and misconstrued one. 

10. The statements made in affidavit-in-opposition by the Respondent No. 2 are as follows:-
a. That on the date of lodgement of the FIR, M. Wahidul Haque, Abu Hena Mostafa Kamal and Saiful Haque were arrested by the investigating agency and they were forwarded to the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka with a prayer for remand of the petitioner. 
b That the Metropolitan Magistrate, Court No. 25, Dhaka granted bail to the accused M. Wahidul Haque and Abu Hena Mostafa Kamal and allowed the prayer for remand of accused Md Saiful Haque, that is, the writ petitioner. 
c. That after remand, the accused Saiful Haque, that is, the writ petitioner made a confessional statement under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. আমার একজন বন্ধু আছে। সে পাকিস্তানে জন্গ্রহণ করে এবং কানাডিয়ান নাগরিক । আমি ব্যবসা শুরু করি ২০১১ সাল হতে তখন হতে আমি এবি ব্যাংক এর ক্লাইন্ট ২০১৩ সালে সেপ্টম্বর মাসে আমার সাথে এবি ব্যাংক এর চেয়ারম্যান ওয়াহিদুল হক এর মিটিং হয়। তখন তিনি আমাকে জানান যে এবি ব্যাংক এর জন্য তারা বিদেশী বিনিয়োগকারী খুজছেন এবং উনি জানতে চান আমি কোন বিদেশী বিনিয়োগকারী চিনি কিনা যারা এবি ব্যাংক এর বিষয়ে আ্গ্রহী হবেন। তখন আমি তাক��� আমার বন্ধু খুররাম আব্দুলাহ এর কথা জানাই । খুররাম আব্দুলাহ তখন দুবাই ইসলামিক ব্যাংক এর শরিয়াহ বোর্ডের চেয়ারম্যান ছিল । আমার মাধ্যমে ওয়াহিদুল হক এর খুররাম আব্দুলাহ এর সাথে যোগাযোগ হয়। এরপর ওয়াহিদুল হক এবং এবি ব্যাংক এর হেড অব ফরেন এক্সচেঞ্জ টিম এর আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামাল ও এবি ব্যাংক এর কয়েকজন কর্মকর্তা দুবাই সফর করে আমার বন্ধু খুররাম আব্দুলাহ এর সাথে মিটিং এর কথা জানায়। এর কিছুদিন পর এম ওয়াহিদুল হক ও আবুহেনা মোস্তফা কামাল দুবাই গিয়ে হায়াত রিজেন্সি হোটেল জনাব খুররাম আব্দুলাহ এর সাথে বিনিয়োগের বিভিন্ন বিষয় নিয়ে মিটিং করে মর্মে খুররাম আব্দুলাহ আমাকে টেলিফোনে জানান পরবর্তীতে মোঃ ওয়াহিদুল হক এর সাথে খুররাম আব্দুলাহ এর মোবাইলে অনেকবার কথাবার্তা হয় এবং ইমেইলে আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামালের সাথে খুররাম আব্দুলাহ এর চুক্তির খসড়া নিয়ে একাধিকবার যোগাযোগ হয় । উক্ত ই-মেইল এর সিসি এম ওয়াহিদুল হক ও আমাকে দেওয়া হতো। ২০১৩ সালের নভেম্বর এর প্রথম সপ্তাহে এম ওয়াহিদুল হক ও আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামাল পুনরায় দুবাই ষায় এবং খুররাম আন্দুলাহ এর সাথে মিটিং করে চুক্তি বিষয়ে ফাইনাল কথাবার্তা হয় যা পরবর্তীতে খুররাম আব্দুলাহ আমাকে অধহিত করেন । মিটিং শেষে দেশে ফিরে চুক্তিতে স্বাক্ষর করে দুবাই পাঠিয়ে দেন মর্মে খুররম আবুলাহ আমাকে জানায় এবং চুক্তি স্ক্যান কপি আমার মেইলে পাঠায় । খুররম আব্দুলাহ এর পক্ষ হতে চুক্তি স্বাক্ষর করে এবি ব্যাংক এ পাঠায় । এবি ব্যাংক উভয়পক্ষ স্বাক্ষরিত চুক্তির কপি আমার মেইলে এ পাঠায় ।২০১৪ সালের ফেব্রুয়ারীর প্রথম সপ্তাহে এম ওয়াহিদুল হক ও আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামাল দুবাই যান দুবাই এডিসিবি এর কথিত হিসাবটি যৌথ স্বাক্ষরের মাধ্যমে পরিচালনার জন্য । দেশে ফেরত এসে এম ওয়াহিদুল হক ও আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামাল এর নির্দেশে দুবাই এডিসিবি ব্যাংক এর চ্যাংবাউ জেনারেল ট্রেডিং এলএমসি এর এ্যাকাউন্ট এ ২০ মিলিয়ন মার্কিন ডলার এবি ব্যাংক হতে পাঠিয়ে দেয়া হয়। যা পরবর্তীতে খুররম আব্দুলাহ আমাকে মোবাইল ফোনের মাধ্যমে অবহিত করে । চুক্তির শর্ত ছিল এ এ্যাকাউন্ট পিজিএফ নামীয় প্রতিষ্ঠান খুররম আব্দুলাহ এর মাধ্যমে এবি ব্যাংক এর এ্যাকাউন্ট এ পাঠাবে । কিন্তু এবি ব্যাংক এর হিসাবে টাকা না আসার কারণে এবি ব্যাংক এর আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামার খুররম আব্দুলাহ এর সাথে বিভিন্ন সময় ই-মেইলে যোগাযোগ করে এবং এর কপি আমাকে দেয় । ২০১৪ সালের আগস্ট মাসে আমার উপস্থিতিতে হোটেল ওয়েষ্টিন এ এম ওয়াহিদুল হক, আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামাল ও খুররম আব্দুলাহ এর মিটিং হয়। এ মিটিং এ খুররম আব্দুলাহ আশ্বস্ত করেন যে খুব শীপ্বই পিজিএফ ৮০ মার্কিন ডলার ফেরত পাঠাবে । এরপর দীর্ঘদিন যাবৎ টাকা না আসায় এম ওয়াহিদুল হক ও আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামাল ২০১৪ সালের ডিসেম্বর মাসে দুবাই যান যৌথ স্বাক্ষরিত Account সম্পর্কে তারা দুবাই গিয়ে জানতে পারে ঐ Account টি যৌথ স্বাক্ষরিত ছিলনা এবং উক্ত Account হতে পে অর্ডার এর মাধ্যমে ২০ মিলিয়ন ডলার উত্তোলন করে Account বন্ধ করে দেয়া হয়েছে । তখন তারা খুররম আব্দুলাহকে না পেয়ে আমাকে ফোন করে । তখন আমি খুররমকে জানালে সেই দুবাই গিয়ে এম ওয়াহিদুল হক ও আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামালের সাথে মিটিং করে। এবং বিষয়টি সুরাহা করার জন্য আশ্বস্ত করলে এম ওয়াহিদুল হক ও আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামাল দেশে চলে আসে । এরপর খুররম আব্দুলাহ আমাকে মোবাইল এর মাধ্যমে জানায় যে চেনবাউ এর সংশ্লিষ্ট Account টির মালিক কানাডিয়ান নাগরিক জনৈক আবদুস সামাদ খান। এবং আব্দুস সামাদ খান ২০ মিলিয়ন ডলার উত্তোলন করে নিয়েছে। তখন আমি থুররম আব্দুলাহ কে এবি ব্যাংক এর সাথে টাকা উদ্ধারের বিষয়ে মিটিং ২৫-১-২০১৫ তারিখে লন্ডনে আমার উপস্থিতিতে এম ওয়াহিদুল হক, আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামাল, ব্যারিস্টার আফজাল উদ্দিন আহমেদ, খুররম আব্দুলাহ ও আব্দুস সামাদ খান এর মিটিং হয়। এ মিটিং এ একটি চুক্তি হয় যেখানে আব্দুস সামাদ খান স্বাক্ষর করে স্বীকার করে ৬ মাসের মধ্যে ২০ মিলিয়ন ডলার এবি ব্যাংক এর 4১০০০৪ এ ফেরত দিবে । কিন্তু সে টাকা ফেরত প্রদান করে নাই । খুররম আব্দুলাহ আমার বন্ধু হবার কারণে আমি ঘটনা সম্পর্কে অবহিত আছি। টাকা বিদেশে পাঠানোর বিষয়ে আমার কোন সংশ্লিষ্টতা নাই । এবি ব্যাংক এর আমি কেউ নই । আমি একজন গ্রাহক মাত্র । এবি ব্যাংক এব সাবেক চেয়ারম্যান এম ওয়াহিদুল হক ও ব্যবস্থাপনা পরিচালক আবু হেনা মোস্তফা কামাল ব্যক্তি উদ্যোগে ব্যাংক এর নিয়ম নীতি বহির্ভতভাবে ২০ মিলিয়ন আব্দুস সামাদ খানকে চাপ প্রয়োগ করলে উক্ত টাকা উদ্ধার করা সম্ভব। এই আমার জবানবন্দি।

We have gone through the writ petition along with the materials annexed therewith and the affidavit-in-opposition together with materials appended therein, perused the writ petition and the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the learned Advocate for the Anti-Corruption Commission and also considered the submissions advanced by the respective parties. It may be mentioned that a money laundering case has been filed against the petitioner and others alleging, inter alia, that the accused of the case, in collaboration with each other, laundered 20 million US dollar to an account of ADCB Bank, Dubai from AB Bank, Bangladesh through 3-transaction swifts without the permission of Bangladesh Bank. 24. Before coming to a decision in this matter, we want to make a brief discussion on the offence of money laundering. It may be noted that the money laundering is a serious financial crime which is committed and carried out by individuals, corporations or by organized crime groups for the purpose of generating huge profits. In order to give colour of legitimacy, these profits are laundered by the criminals. Corrupt public officials launder their ill-gotten bribes and kick-backs to give them the colour of legitimacy. If the money laundering offences are unchecked, money-laundering can destabilize the financial system and undermine the development efforts in emerging markets. It weakens the social fabric and collective ethical standards. Money-laundering can adversely affect economies by making interest and exchange rates more volatile changing the demand for cash, and by causing inflation in economies where criminals are engaged in business. The siphoning away of huge volumes of money from normal economic growth poses a real danger to the economies and affects the stability of the national and global market. It empowers corruption and organized crime. Criminals have to disguise the origin of investments out of the proceeds of crime. Money-laundering involves, at some points, a conversion process, with the objective to give the appearance that the money has a legitimate source, so that it raises no suspicions when it is finally turned into apparently legitimate wealth. 

25. The money laundering often involves a complex series of transactions but it generally includes the following three basic steps: 
1. Placement —It involves introduction of the proceeds of crime into the financial system. 
2. Layering—This involves formation of complex layers of financial transactions which distance the illicit proceeds from their source and disguise the audit trail. 
3. Integration—This involves investment in the legitimate economy so that the money gets the colour of legitimacy. 

26. The money laundering is also termed as white collar crimes. The white collar crimes are often committed by a person of responsibility, respectability and high social status in the course of their occupation. These non-violent crimes are usually committed in commercial institutions for financial gain. Many white-collar crimes are especially difficult to prosecute because the perpetrators use sophisticated means to conceal their activities through a series of complex transactions. 

27. Anyway, the investigation of the case pending against the petitioner and others is underway. The purpose and object of the enactment of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 is to prevent corruption and other corrupt practices in the country. And the purpose and object of the money laundering Protirodh Ain, 2012 is to prevent the money laundering offences along with other related offences usually committed through suspicious transactions and other predicate offences as enunciated in section 2(Fa), 2(Ja) and 2(Sa) of the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain, 2012. The purpose and object of the investigation is to unearth the perpetrators who are involved in the commission of money laundering offences and other schedule offences and to bring them to justice collecting necessary papers and articles on which the prosecution proposes to rely. It is obvious duty of the Court to give effect to the will and inbuilt policy of the Legislature as discernible from the object and scheme of the enactment and language employed therein. The normal practice of the court is that when any accused is involved in financial crimes like money laundering of a huge amount of money, the judges do not feel encouraged to enlarge that type of accused on bail during investigation of the case mainly on an apprehension that the accused may flee away from the case and he may also tamper the evidence and materials required for making prima facie case for the prosecution. The main argument of the petitioner is that the Respondent No. 3, that is, one Director of the Commission seized the passport of the petitioner without having any order from the competent authority or from any Court of law and as such, the order for seizure of the passport of the petitioner is illegal, without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the same is also violative of Article 36 of the Constitution of the People' Republic of Bangladesh. 31. In view of submissions and counter submissions of the respective parties, it is worthwhile to give a brief look at the power and function of the investigating officer as stipulated in section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. When the investigating officer takes up a case for investigation, he is to collect the relevant papers and documents on which the prosecution proposes to rely on them and at the same time he will record the statements of the witnesses under Sub-section 3 of section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, whom the prosecution proposes to examine as it witnesses. After holding investigation into the case and after completion of investigation, the investigating officer shall forward the investigating report along with the papers and document including the 161 statements of the witnesses to the Magistrate. Upon receiving the investigating report, the learned Magistrate shall decide as to whether the case is triable by the learned Magistrate or by the learned Sessions Judge. The Learned Magistrate shall take cognizance of the offence against the accused under section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure if it is triable by the Magistrate. If the case appears to be triable by the learned Sessions Judge, in that case, the learned Magistrate shall forward the case record along with the documents and articles, if any which are to be produced in evidence. 

32. Similar power and authority of investigation as has been given to the investigating officer under the Code of Criminal Procedure has also been given to the investigating officer of the Commission/Commission under section 20 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. Sub-section (1) of section 20 of the Act stipulates that notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, the offences under this Act and specified in its Schedule shall be inquired into or investigated only by the Commission. Sub-section (2) of section 20 of the Act indicates that the Commission may, by notification in the official Gazette, empower any of its subordinate officer to inquire into or investigate the offences mentioned in sub-section (1). Sub-section(3) of section 20 of the Act contemplates that an officer empowered under sub-section (2) shall have the power of an officer-in-charge of a Police Station in respect of inquiry and investigation of an offence, which came into force on 21-6-2016 by Act No. 25 of 2016. In the present case at hand, the Respondent No. 3, Director of the Anti-Corruption Commission exercising his power and authority under sections 17, 19 and 20 read with section 2Ka of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 wherein the power and function of the commission for inquiry and investigation has been thoroughly stated and stipulated. The Durnity Daman Commission preserves the power to issue summon, collect document, and record the evidence on which the prosecution proposes to rely. There is no provision in the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 or in the Anti-Corruption Commission Rules, 2007 debarring or preventing the Commission from carrying out inquiry/ investigation/further investigation into the allegations of corruption, bribery, money laundering and other schedule offences and bringing the perpetrator/s to justice. The provision laid down in section 19 (1) (Cha) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 is the residuary power which has been given by the legislature to the Durnity Daman Commission in order to fulfil the purpose and object of the enactment appearing in the preamble of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, which is quoted as under:

34. It may be mentioned that the purpose and object of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 is quite different than the purpose and object of the Bangladesh Passport Order, 1973. Accordingly, the provisions of the Bangladesh Passport Order, 1973 are not applicable to the matters arising out of the administrative action /order of the Commission under the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, which is evident from section 2 Ka of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 which suggests that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the provisions of this Act shall prevail. Section 17 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 indicates that the Commission may hold inquiry/investigation into any allegation of corruption/schedule offences of the Act on its own motion or on an application made by an aggrieved person or any person on his behalf. The aforesaid statement of law has been affirmed in the cases of Tarique Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 63 DLR (AD) 18, Anti-Corruption Commission, Dhaka vs Abdul Azim reported in 69 DLR (AD) 208 and Anti-Corruption Commission vs Monjur Morshed Khan reported in 64 DLR (AD) 124. Section 19(2) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 contemplates that the Commission may require any person to furnish any information regarding a matter of inquiry or investigation and the person so required shall be bound to furnish such information kept under his custody. Section 20 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 speaks to the effect that notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, the offences under this Act and specified in its schedule shall be inquired into or investigated only by the Commission. The Commission can proceed with the matter of inquiry/investigation into any allegation of corruption, bribery and money laundering independently if the elements of corruption and bribery are there. There is neither any constitutional nor any statutory or any legal bar to conduct an inquiry/investigation into any allegation of corruption/schedule offences of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, by the Commission. As per section 14 of the Money Laundering Protirodh Ain, 2012 read with Rule 18 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Rules, 2007, on the prayer of investigation officer of the Commission, and/or the Commission , the Senior Special Judge Court or the Court before which the case is pending can pass an order for freezing the bank account and for attaching the properties remained within Bangladesh or outside Bangladesh which are acquired and obtained by committing the offence of money laundering or by the proceeds of money laundering. The passport of the petitioner was validly given to the petitioner by the concerned department of government under Article 7(2) of the Bangladesh Passport Order, 1973. It may be stated that passport is an official document issued by a government certifying the holders identity and citizenship and entitling them to travel under its protection to and from foreign countries. Admittedly, the passport of the petitioner is a valid document given by the government and that passport has not been obtained or acquired by the proceeds of the money laundering offences. 

35. Article 36 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh reads that, 
"Subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the public interest, every citizen shall have the right to move freely throughout Bangladesh, to reside and settle in any place therein and to leave and re-enter Bangladesh." 

36. It is true that for the right guaranteed in Article 36 of the Constitution, a citizen can freely move throughout Bangladesh and to leave and re-inter Bangladesh, but that right is not an absolute one and is subject to reasonable restriction imposed by law. However, the government in the interest of sovereignty, integrity or security of Bangladesh or in the public interest can impound/revoke a passport of a citizen if it appears to it necessary to do it, but of course assigning reasons whatsoever in support of impounding/revoking the passport under the Bangladesh Passport Order, 1973. Similarly the Commission can seize the passport of a citizen if that person commits the schedule offences of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 if there is an apprehension to it that the person involved in the commission of schedule offences may flee away from the country and tamper the materials/ evidence on which the prosecution will rely. We have stated earlier that the petitioner in collaboration with other accused laundered 20 million US dollar equivalent to approximately Tk. 1,696,168,800 to Dubai from AB Bank, which is a prima-facie case of a serious financial crime and transnational money laundering case. The aforesaid fact definitely causes an apprehension to the effect that the petitioner may flee away from Bangladesh and he may also commit tampering on the evidence and materials if he is allowed to go abroad at this stage. Under the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case, the seizure of the petitioner's passport by the Respondent No. 3 does not appear to be violative of Article 36 of the Constitution. 

37. Accordingly, we are of the view that the investigating officer/Commission is not required to submit any application before the concerned court wherein the case is pending, for seizure of the passport of a person/accused who is involved in the commission of money laundering offence and other schedule offences of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, rather the investigating officer/Commission has ample and unfettered power and authority to seize the passport of a person/accused who is involved in the commission of money laundering and other schedule offences of the Act in order to fulfil the purpose and object of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. 

38. Since the money laundering case against the petitioner and others is pending before the Learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Dhaka, the petitioner has an opportunity to file an application for release of the passport before that court. Since the petitioner has alternative remedy, the writ petition filed by the petitioner is not maintainable in the eye of law. 

39. As per statements made in the writ petition that the petitioner has been suffering from some chronic diseases and he is required to undergo a thorough investigation as well as surgery as suggested by the specialist doctor of SAMITIVEJ HOSPITAL, BANGKOK. The petitioner has not stated the name of the diseases in the application. However, as per submission of the learned Advocate for the Anti-Corruption Commission the diseases as apparent from annexure-E series, are treatable in Bangladesh. 
Accordingly, the statements with regard to the chronic diseases are not satisfactory. Furthermore, these are not the issues to be decided in this writ petition. The fact of diseases may come as an aid to come to a decision when the substantive prayer of the petitioner, by setting aside the impugned order of seizure of the passport of the petitioner, is liable to be sustained both factually and legally. In the view of the above discussions, we are led to hold the view that there is no bar to seize the passport of a person/accused who is involved in the commission of the schedule offences, by the Commission during inquiry/investigation/further investigation into the allegation of the schedule offences of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 if the circumstances demand to do the same and we do not find any illegality, infirmity and impropriety in the seizure of the petitioner's passport by the Respondent No.3 and the same deserves to be maintained. 

40. Having considered all the facts and circumstances, the submissions of the respective parties, the proposition of laws and the discussions made above, we do not find any merit in this Rule. 

41. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged. 

42. In consequence thereof, the ad-interim order dated 31-5-2018 of this Court directing the Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to release the petitioner's passport is recalled and vacated. 

43. The Investigating Officer/Commission is directed to conclude the investigation and to submit the investigation report as early as possible preferably within 6 (six) months from the date of receipt of this judgement and order. 

Let a copy of this judgment and order be communicated to the learned judge of the concerned court below, the Chairman of the Commission and the other respondents at once. 

End.
